claims.text: Long-term structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles at high temperature is governed by their ability to form and maintain a thin self-passivating surface layer.
A surface oxide or carbide layer kinetically restricts surface segregation.
A surface oxide or carbide layer kinetically restricts nanoparticle sintering.
High configurational entropy stabilizes uniform mixing and a solid-solution phase in the alloy core.
Controlled surface passivation provides a barrier to fast atomic diffusion during service and thereby preserves a single-phase core.
The as-synthesized HEA nanoparticles are single-phase, chemically homogeneous solid solutions.
The nanoparticles have a high density of surface atoms that are prone to reconstruction during thermal exposure.
Low-oxygen annealing or mild post-synthesis deposition can be used to pre-form a sub-nanometer oxide or carbide shell.
The relevant structural mediator is a coherent surface passivation layer of controlled thickness.
The passivation layer minimizes atomic diffusion and surface reconstruction.
Suppressing surface diffusion and reconstruction kinetically traps the high-entropy configuration and limits sintering and phase segregation.
Passivated nanoparticles will exhibit less particle coarsening than untreated nanoparticles during high-temperature exposure.
Passivated nanoparticles will show less compositional segregation, measured as smaller changes in surface elemental ratios.
Passivated nanoparticles will preserve phase homogeneity better than untreated nanoparticles.
Clean, untreated HEA nanoparticle surfaces are prone to rapid sintering and chemical segregation at service temperatures.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply to near-equiatomic HEAs containing typically five or more elements in similar molar ratios.
The mechanism applies only while the atmosphere and temperature do not completely oxidize or otherwise transform the passivation layer.
With a controlled atmosphere, the proposed passivation mechanism can remain applicable up to approximately 1173 K in catalysis and 1923 K in thermoelectric service.
The optimal chemistry and thickness of the passivation layer are not established and may depend on alloy composition and functional-performance constraints.
